extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate executives, and students of public opinion/propaganda
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and professional standards for the practice of public relations (the public relations counsel): roles, methods, ethics, audience analysis, and use of mass-psychology and publicity techniques to shape public opinion and acceptance of products, policies, or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the public relations counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel interprets enterprises and ideas to the public and interprets the public to promulgators of ideas; concerned with courses of action, doctrines, systems and opinions, and with tangible products and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions like an adviser or lawyer focused on public contacts: examines product, markets, public reactions, employees' attitudes, and distribution cooperation; shapes the client's actions so they will gain public interest, approval and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive client analysis before action
rubrics_metrics.description: First efforts are devoted to analyzing the client's problems and making sure what is offered is something the public accepts or can be brought to accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an institution is 'basically unsound' he should not futilely attempt to sell it; he may advise organizational modification (examples: orphan asylum reorganized on 'cottage plan'; corset makers advised to offer a healthier girdle; railroad urged to add a fast train for prestige).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience (public) analysis and segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the public: identify groups which must be reached and the leaders through whom to approach them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study social, economic, geographical, age, doctrinal, language, cultural groups to determine division lines and selecting group leaders as communication channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate internal policies prior to publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Only after client and public analysis are collated should policies governing general practice, procedure and habits of the client in public contact be formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies must be agreed upon before moving to publicity steps; in some cases once policies and public understanding are aligned, the counsel's work may be finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of communication channels appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the full range of communication media to reach the public: conversation, letters, the stage, motion pictures, radio, lecture platform, magazines, daily newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel is not primarily an advertising man but will advocate advertising when indicated and often supplement an advertising agency's work to avoid duplication or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous work and vigilance; rumor and information management
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations often require continuous, systematic, and frank information; counsel must maintain constant vigilance since inadequate or false information can have enormous consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deal effectively with rumors and suspicions: stop them at source, counter promptly with correct or more complete information via the most effective channels, or establish relations of confidence so rumors cannot take root; a single false rumor can cause large financial loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is developing an ethical code: counsel should refuse dishonest clients, fraudulent products, or antisocial causes, and avoid conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While presenting a client's case in its best light, the counsel should be candid and not attempt to fool the public; propaganda material should be clearly labeled as to source so editors know its origin and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse hopeless or conflicting engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept a client whose case is believed hopeless, whose product is unmarketable, or whose interests conflict with another client's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel's reputation depends on honesty and usefulness; accepting such clients undermines long-term effectiveness and professional standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic professional ideal: reduce waste by aligning product and public
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of the profession is pragmatic: to make the producer understand what the public wants and make the public understand the producer, thereby eliminating waste and friction when industry makes things the public does not want or the public misunderstands offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: telephone companies explaining exchange-name choices to stimulate cooperation; public relations used to build understanding between educators and educated, government and people, charities and contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic study of mass psychology (scientific method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern propaganda bases operations upon definite knowledge drawn from direct observation of the group mind and on principles shown to be relatively constant; the propagandist studies material in a laboratory spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools such as clipping services, scouts, and personal observation to determine trends (e.g., which product features are losing appeal); however, accept inherent limits and margins of error—propaganda is not an exact science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage group leaders to influence wider groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Influencing leaders—whether conscious or not—automatically influences the groups they sway; the group mind tends to follow trusted leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and persuade opinion leaders (e.g., physicians recommending bacon increased sales) rather than direct appeals to every individual; use respected figures in staged events to project ideas to wider publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clichés, associative processes and staged publicity to change customs
rubrics_metrics.description: When the herd must 'think for itself' it relies on clichés and associative images; the modern propagandist exploits associative processes and staged events to create acceptance and demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create exhibitions, competitions, ceremonies, and use prominent authorities and celebrities to associate ideas with prestige (examples: music-room exhibitions with famous violinists to sell pianos; Jackson Heights development openings; Ivory soap sculpture contests to involve children and schools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances to remove sales resistance (not merely direct appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than direct assault on sales resistance, modern salesmanship removes resistance by modifying customs and creating emotional currents favorable to the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop supporting social or architectural trends, enlist influential professionals (architects, decorators), stage events, and use associative prestige so desire appears to be the purchaser's own idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure product/idea is fundamentally marketable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting publicity, ensure the product or idea is essentially sound and capable of being accepted by the public; counsel should not attempt to sell an unmarketable commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product or policy is unsound, advise modification (e.g., corset → healthier girdle) or decline to attempt to create false acceptance; futile publicity for unsound offerings wastes resources and harms reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand hidden/unconscious motives behind public behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Men (and the masses) are often motivated by impulses, habits and unconscious desires; successful propaganda requires understanding these deeper motives rather than accepting stated reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate symbolic or compensatory motives (Freudian insights) behind choices—e.g., buying a car may symbolize success—so campaigns target true motivations, not superficial justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and cost-driven concentration of propaganda functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reaching and persuading masses is expensive, functions of propaganda tend to concentrate in the hands of specialists—the public relations counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emergence of the profession and new nomenclature reflects increasing complexity of modern life and the need for continuous, expert management of public contacts and opinion.
